global.title: The Future of Cooling in Southeast Asia
global.limit: A projection to 2040 under stated policies, not a forecast; it changes with efficiency rules.
global.finding: Southeast Asia’s air conditioners could rise from 40 million in 2017 to 300 million in 2040, half of them in Indonesia. Without more efficient units, cooling could drive as much as 30% of the region’s peak electricity demand.

global.title: The Future of Cooling
global.limit: A projection to 2050 that assumes current trends; better efficiency changes it.
global.finding: The world’s stock of air conditioners is set to grow from 1.6 billion to 5.6 billion by 2050, and the energy they use to triple, unless efficiency improves.

soil.title: Investigating soil moisture–climate interactions in a changing climate: a review
soil.limit: Explains a general mechanism; how strong it is varies by region and season.
soil.finding: Reviews the evidence that dry soils amplify hot temperatures: with less water to evaporate, more of the sun’s energy goes into heating the air.

ice.by: Ibel, Mölg and Sommer, The Cryosphere, 2025
ice.title: Tropical glaciers on Puncak Jaya close to extinction
ice.scale: One glacier field, satellite and field data
ice.limit: One site; the 2030 date is the authors’ estimate.
ice.finding: Puncak Jaya’s glaciers, the last in Southeast Asia, have lost more than 99% of their area since 1850 and about 65% since 2018. About 0.165 km² remained in 2024, and they will very likely be gone around 2030.

ice.title: Water, ice, society, and ecosystems in the Hindu Kush Himalaya: an outlook
ice.limit: Volume losses are projections that depend on how much warming happens.
ice.finding: Glaciers lost ice 65% faster in the 2010s than in the decade before. At 1.5–2 °C of warming, glaciers across the region lose 30–50% of their volume by 2100.

fire.title: The Cost of Fire: An Economic Analysis of Indonesia’s 2015 Fire Crisis
fire.limit: One exceptional year, in an El Niño; costs in other years differ.
fire.finding: Indonesia’s forest and peatland fires of June to October 2015 cost the country an estimated US$16.1 billion.

fire.title: Spreading like Wildfire: The Rising Threat of Extraordinary Landscape Fires
fire.limit: Global projections; not broken down for Asian countries.
fire.finding: Climate change and land-use change are making wildfires worse. Extreme fires are projected to rise by up to 14% by 2030 and 50% by the end of the century.

cooling.by: Salamanca et al., Journal of Geophysical Research, 2014 (summary by Arizona State University)
cooling.title: Excess heat from air conditioners causes higher nighttime temperatures
cooling.limit: A desert city outside Asia; the size of the effect in humid Asian cities is not measured here.
cooling.reading: We use it for the mechanism, not the number: waste heat from cooling warms the street outside.
cooling.finding: In a Phoenix heatwave, waste heat from air conditioners raised night-time air temperatures by more than 1 °C in parts of the city.

cooling.title: The Future of Cooling
cooling.limit: A projection to 2050 that assumes current trends.
cooling.finding: China, India and Indonesia are expected to account for half of the world’s air conditioners by 2050.

cooling.title: Beating the Heat: Tamil Nadu Heat Mitigation Strategy
cooling.limit: Land surface temperature, not the air temperature people breathe; the two differ.
cooling.finding: Chennai’s built-up area more than doubled between 2000 and 2020, and night-time land surface temperatures in its urban areas run about 2 °C higher than on its peri-urban edges.

cooling.by: Cooling Singapore, citing Chow and Roth, 2006
cooling.title: Cooling Singapore: digital urban climate twin
cooling.type: Research programme summary of a peer-reviewed study
cooling.limit: The 7 °C is a maximum on calm, clear nights, not a typical night.
cooling.finding: Singapore’s commercial centre has measured up to about 7 °C warmer than its outskirts on calm, clear nights.

energywater.by: World Bank estimate, reported by AFP via The Manila Times, 2023
energywater.title: Power crisis cost Vietnam $1.4B
energywater.type: News report of a World Bank early estimate
energywater.limit: An early estimate reported in the press; drought and demand both played a part.
energywater.finding: Heatwaves in May and June 2023 pushed up demand while hydropower reservoirs ran low, and rolling blackouts hit northern Vietnam. The World Bank’s early estimate put the cost at about US$1.4 billion, roughly 0.3% of GDP.

energywater.title: 40% of India’s thermal power plants are in water-scarce areas, threatening shutdowns
energywater.limit: Data from before 2017; plants and water rules have changed since.
energywater.finding: 14 of India’s 20 largest thermal utilities shut down at least once for lack of water between 2013 and 2016. Water shortages cost 14 TWh of power in 2016.

pumping.by: Minderhoud et al., Environmental Research Communications, 2020
pumping.title: Groundwater extraction may drown mega-delta
pumping.limit: Sinking rates vary across the delta; the top rate is not everywhere.
pumping.finding: Groundwater pumping has sped up the sinking of the Mekong delta, to more than 2.5 cm a year in some areas.

pumping.title: Satellite-based estimates of groundwater depletion in India
pumping.limit: An older period; it measures water lost, not the heat link itself.
pumping.reading: The heat link is ours: hotter, drier seasons raise the pull on groundwater that this study measures.
pumping.finding: Satellites show Rajasthan, Punjab and Haryana lost 109 km³ of groundwater between 2002 and 2008, mainly to irrigation, while rainfall stayed close to normal.

clinic.title: The 2024 report of the Lancet Countdown on health and climate change
clinic.limit: A global figure; it does not give Asia’s share.
clinic.finding: Heat-related deaths among people over 65 reached a record 167% above the 1990s level in 2023.

clinic.by: Hess et al., Journal of Environmental and Public Health, 2018
clinic.title: Pilot evaluation of the impact of India’s first heat action plan on all-cause mortality
clinic.scale: One city, before and after the plan
clinic.limit: A pilot evaluation; other changes over the same years could explain part of the drop.
clinic.finding: After Ahmedabad’s heat action plan prepared hospitals and warned the public, an estimated 1,190 deaths a year were avoided.

poverty.title: Climate change and heat stress: impacts on home-based workers and street vendors in Bangkok
poverty.limit: Self-reported, from workers in one city.
poverty.finding: In a survey of informal workers in Bangkok, nearly 80% had cut their hours because of heat, and 75% of home-based workers lost at least one day of work a month to their own or a family member’s heat illness.

poverty.by: OECD Economics Department, Working Paper No. 1828, 2024
poverty.title: The heat is on: Heat stress, productivity and adaptation among firms
poverty.where: 23 advanced economies, including Japan and Korea
poverty.limit: Rich economies with formal firms; informal work in South and Southeast Asia is not covered.
poverty.reading: If formal firms in rich economies lose this much, the losses where work is outdoors and informal are likely larger, but that is not measured here.
poverty.finding: Across 2.7 million firms in 23 advanced economies, including Japan and Korea, ten extra days above 35 °C cut yearly labour productivity by 0.3%, and over 1.5% above 40 °C. Very humid places lost 0.75%, more than double the average. Korea has already lost about 0.15% of productivity to added heat since the early 2000s.

poverty.by: World Bank, 2022, reported by Down To Earth
poverty.title: Climate Investment Opportunities in India’s Cooling Sector
poverty.type: Agency report, reported by the press
poverty.limit: A broad estimate of heat-exposed work, not a count of workers harmed.
poverty.finding: Up to three-quarters of India’s workforce, about 380 million people, depend on heat-exposed labour, work that produces nearly half of the country’s GDP.

poverty.title: Working on a warmer planet
poverty.limit: A projection to 2030 at about 1.5 °C of warming.
poverty.finding: Heat stress is projected to cost 2.2% of all working hours by 2030, equal to 80 million full-time jobs. South Asia is among the worst hit, losing about 5% of working hours.

poverty.title: The 2024 report of the Lancet Countdown on health and climate change
poverty.limit: Potential hours and income at risk, not hours actually lost.
poverty.finding: Heat exposure put a record 512 billion potential labour hours at risk in 2023, with potential income losses of US$835 billion.

poverty.title: An Unsustainable Life: the impact of heat on health and the economy of Bangladesh
poverty.limit: Combines survey and modelling; the money value is an upper estimate.
poverty.finding: Heat-related illness cost Bangladesh 250 million workdays in 2024, worth up to US$1.78 billion, about 0.4% of GDP. Since 1980 the ‘feels-like’ temperature has risen by 4.5 °C.

debt.title: Microfinance debt in Cambodia
debt.limit: Shows how heavy debt is; it does not measure the part heat plays.
debt.finding: Cambodia’s average microloan was over US$5,800 in 2024, more than four times the country’s median annual income per person.

debt.by: Selvaraj, Farooqui and Karan, BMJ Open, 2018
debt.title: Quantifying the financial burden of households’ out-of-pocket payments on medicines in India
debt.limit: Older data on all medicine costs, not heat illness alone.
debt.reading: We read it as the hole a heat illness can fall into; the study does not single out heat.
debt.finding: Medicine costs alone were catastrophic for 11.2% of Indian households in 2011–12, about 29 million households.

debt.by: American Red Cross, Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, Nepal Red Cross Society and Bangladesh Red Crescent Society, 2026
debt.title: The lived experiences of vulnerable populations in the context of extreme heat: five cities in Nepal and Bangladesh
debt.where: Five cities in Nepal and Bangladesh
debt.limit: Reported experiences; it does not measure how often loans followed heat.
debt.finding: In a survey of more than 2,000 residents of five cities, heat harmed health, cut incomes and working hours, and pushed some households towards high-interest loans. Women and people with disabilities faced the hardest trade-offs between health, work and care.

energypoverty.title: Chilling Prospects: Global Access to Cooling Gaps 2023
energypoverty.limit: Risk of lacking cooling, estimated from income, power and heat data, not a direct survey.
energypoverty.finding: 1.12 billion of the rural and urban poor are at high risk because they lack access to cooling.

displacement.title: Groundswell Part II
displacement.limit: A worst-case scenario to 2050; covers all climate drivers, not heat alone.
displacement.finding: Without action, as many as 49 million people in East Asia and the Pacific could become internal climate migrants by 2050.

displacement.title: Groundswell Part 2: Acting on Internal Climate Migration
displacement.limit: A worst-case scenario to 2050; covers all climate drivers, not heat alone.
displacement.finding: Without action, climate change could force up to 216 million people to move within their own countries by 2050, including about 40 million in South Asia.

school.by: Park, Goodman, Hurwitz and Smith, American Economic Journal: Economic Policy, 2020
school.title: Heat and Learning
school.limit: US schools and tests; the size of the effect in Asian classrooms is not known.
school.reading: We use it for direction: hotter school years mean less learning, and the poorest lose most.
school.finding: Without air conditioning, each 1 °F hotter school year cuts that year’s learning by about 1%, and the losses fall hardest on disadvantaged students.

school.title: Learning interrupted: global snapshot of climate-related school disruptions in 2024
school.scale: Global count from news and official reports
school.limit: Counts students affected by closures or shorter days, not learning lost.
school.finding: Heatwaves disrupted schooling for an estimated 171 million students in 2024. South Asia was the most affected region.

school.title: Thousands of Philippine schools suspend in-person classes due to heat
school.limit: A snapshot of one week, from official figures quoted in the press.
school.finding: In early April 2024, 5,288 schools across the Philippines switched to remote learning as the heat index reached danger levels, affecting more than 3.6 million students.

school.title: Extreme heat forces school closures across Asia, affecting millions of students
school.finding: Bangladesh closed schools for about 33 million children in its April 2024 heatwave, and Cambodia cut the school day by two hours.

sleep.title: Singapore’s Third National Climate Change Study (V3)
sleep.limit: End-of-century figures depend on the emissions scenario.
sleep.finding: Singapore averaged 76 warm nights a year (above 26.3 °C) over the last 40 years; by the end of the century such nights could occur on most nights of the year.

sleep.title: Rising temperatures erode human sleep globally
sleep.limit: Most wearers live in higher-income countries; the poorest, who sleep hottest, are under-represented.
sleep.finding: Data from 47,628 people in 68 countries shows hot nights shorten sleep, with bigger losses for older people and in lower-income countries.

sleep.by: Thompson et al., The Lancet Planetary Health, 2023 (summary by Imperial College London)
sleep.title: Ambient temperature and mental health: a systematic review and meta-analysis
sleep.limit: Shows an association, not proof of cause.
sleep.finding: A review of 114 studies links higher temperatures with poorer mental health, including higher suicide rates.

sleep.by: Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW), 2025
sleep.title: How Extreme Heat is Impacting India: Assessing District-level Heat Risk
sleep.limit: Based on reanalysis data, which can miss very local differences.
sleep.finding: Over the last decade, nearly 70% of India’s districts gained five or more very warm nights each summer, while only about 28% saw a similar rise in very hot days. Mumbai gained 15 very warm nights a summer, and Bengaluru 11.

sleep.title: Beating the Heat: Tamil Nadu Heat Mitigation Strategy
sleep.finding: Tamil Nadu’s summer minimum temperatures have risen by about 0.75 °C since the 1980s, and about 56% of its people now live where summer nights are warmer than the 1981–2011 average.

deadgreen.by: Esperon-Rodriguez et al., Nature Climate Change, 2022
deadgreen.title: Climate change increases global risk to urban forests
deadgreen.limit: Compares climate to each species’ natural range; trees can survive outside it with care.
deadgreen.finding: Of 3,129 tree and shrub species in 164 cities, 56% already face temperatures beyond those in their natural range, rising to about 76% by 2050 under a mid-range warming scenario. Risk is highest in low-latitude cities such as New Delhi and Singapore.

deadgreen.by: Hansen et al., chapter 10 in Nature-Based Solutions for Cities, 2023
deadgreen.title: Planning and maintaining nature-based solutions: Berlin, Jakarta, Melbourne and Santiago
deadgreen.limit: The tree figures are from Berlin; Asian evidence on tree loss in heat is thinner.
deadgreen.reading: We take the lesson that new trees need years of water and care, wherever they are planted.
deadgreen.finding: Drought stops urban trees from cooling through transpiration. In one Berlin park more than 500 of 870 new trees died within ten years despite watering, and Berlin cut about 44,000 street trees between 2012 and 2019 while planting about 18,000.

deadgreen.by: Middel et al., Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society
deadgreen.title: 50 Grades of Shade
deadgreen.limit: A desert city; humid cities gain less from shade alone, though shade still cuts radiant heat.
deadgreen.finding: Tree shade sharply lowers the radiant heat people feel by day, which is the cooling lost when trees die.

greendisplace.title: Green gentrification in European and North American cities
greendisplace.where: 28 cities in Europe and North America
greendisplace.limit: No Asian cities in the sample.
greendisplace.reading: We treat it as a warning for Asia’s greening plans, not proof it happens the same way there.
greendisplace.finding: Across 28 cities in 9 countries, greening in the 1990s and 2000s was strongly linked to gentrification between 2000 and 2016 in 17 of them.

greendisplace.by: Wolch, Byrne and Newell, Landscape and Urban Planning, 2014
greendisplace.title: Urban green space, public health and environmental justice: making cities “just green enough”
greendisplace.finding: Green space tends to favour wealthier neighbourhoods, and new parks meant to fix that can raise housing costs and displace the residents they were meant to help. Small, local projects are more likely to reach those who need them.

greendisplace.title: Gentrification, urban informality and displacement in Bangkok
greendisplace.limit: Qualitative; it does not measure how many people moved.
greendisplace.finding: Fieldwork on how recent gentrification in Bangkok, including green urban renewal, affects the city’s lower-income residents.

greendisplace.by: Chapter 3 in Nature-Based Solutions for Cities, 2023
greendisplace.title: Towards just nature-based solutions for cities
greendisplace.limit: A framework for justice, not a measure of harm.
greendisplace.finding: Nature-based solutions can deepen injustice when benefits flow to some and costs, including displacement, fall on others; procedural, distributional and recognition justice all need attention.

squeeze.by: OECD Economics Department, Working Paper No. 1828, 2024
squeeze.title: The heat is on: Heat stress, productivity and adaptation among firms
squeeze.limit: Rich economies; small informal firms in Asia are not covered.
squeeze.finding: Across 2.7 million firms in 23 advanced economies, heat cut the productivity of small firms while medium and large firms showed no loss, and the largest grew revenue about 0.6 points faster than small firms after hot years. Losses lasted up to two years. Restaurants and hotels were hit hard, partly through lower demand.

squeeze.by: Aguilar-Gomez et al., summarised in VoxEU, 2024
squeeze.title: Heatwaves ripple into the financial system
squeeze.type: Research summary of a peer-reviewed study
squeeze.limit: Outside Asia; how Asian banks respond is not yet measured.
squeeze.reading: We read it as a likely pattern for Asian lenders, to be checked against their own loan books.
squeeze.finding: Loan-level bank data from Mexico show that ten extra days of extreme heat in a quarter raise small-business loan delinquency by about 4%, mainly among firms that depend on local customers. Banks then raise rates, ask for more collateral and lend less for two to three quarters.

squeeze.title: Micro-loan asset quality deteriorates in April–June quarter
squeeze.type: News report of an industry statement
squeeze.limit: Heat is one named cause among several, not measured on its own.
squeeze.finding: India’s microfinance industry body said loan quality worsened in April–June 2024, partly because heatwaves cut borrowers’ incomes and lenders’ collections.

squeeze.title: New study finds that microfinance is exacerbating climate precarity and harm in Cambodia
squeeze.limit: About climate shocks in general, not heat alone.
squeeze.finding: A caution for lenders: in Cambodia, researchers found that borrowing to get through climate shocks often delayed the harm rather than removing it, leaving households more indebted for the next shock.

squeeze.by: Greenpeace India and National Hawkers Federation, 2024
squeeze.title: Heatwave Havoc: the toll on Delhi’s street vendors
squeeze.limit: Self-reported, from one city in one season.
squeeze.finding: Of 721 Delhi street vendors surveyed in April and May 2024, 80% saw fewer customers during heatwaves and 49% lost income.

squeeze.by: Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations, reported by Orissa Post, 2024
squeeze.title: Passenger vehicle retail sales dip 7% in June as heatwave curtails showroom visits
squeeze.limit: Dealers’ own account; the link to their loans is not measured.
squeeze.finding: Car dealers said heat cut showroom footfall by about 15% in June 2024, leaving them with 62–67 days of unsold stock against a recommended three weeks. A sign of where to look; the link to their loans is not yet measured.

farmdebt.title: Crop-damaging temperatures increase suicide rates in India
farmdebt.limit: An association that has been debated; it does not prove debt is the cause.
farmdebt.finding: Heat raises suicide rates in India only during the growing season, when it also cuts crop yields, pointing to farm income losses. The findings have been debated.

farmdebt.by: Lobell, Sibley and Ortiz-Monasterio, Nature Climate Change, 2012
farmdebt.title: Extreme heat effects on wheat senescence in India
farmdebt.limit: About wheat only; it shows how models can miss losses.
farmdebt.finding: Days above 34 °C make wheat in northern India age early, and crop models may underestimate yield losses at +2 °C by as much as 50%.

farmdebt.title: Rice yields decline with higher night temperature from global warming
farmdebt.limit: One site; later studies find varied effects across regions.
farmdebt.finding: At the International Rice Research Institute’s farm in the Philippines, rice yields fell by about 10% for each 1 °C rise in growing-season night temperature, while daytime highs had little effect.

invisible.by: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, reply in India’s Rajya Sabha, 6 August 2024
invisible.title: Heat-related illness surveillance, 2021 to July 2024 (Unstarred Question 1693)
invisible.limit: Counts what gets reported; reporting improves over time, so part of the rise is better counting.
invisible.finding: Suspected heatstroke cases rose from 4,481 in 2022 to 48,385 by 28 July 2024, while confirmed heatstroke deaths rose only from 33 to 185.

invisible.title: India likely undercounts heat-related deaths, tempering its response, officials say
invisible.limit: Compares two official counts in one year.
invisible.finding: In 2020, India’s crime records bureau recorded 530 heatstroke deaths while the disaster agency recorded four. Different systems count differently, which makes the full toll hard to see.

invisible.title: Lost in the heat: the critical miscalculation in India’s heatwave mortality data
invisible.limit: Describes how deaths are recorded; it does not estimate the missing number.
invisible.finding: Death certificates usually record only the immediate cause, such as heart failure, so heat as the trigger goes unrecorded.

invisible.by: Ministry of Home Affairs, reply in India’s Lok Sabha, reported by Down To Earth, 2026
invisible.title: India updates disaster list to include heatwaves and lightning after Finance Commission push
invisible.type: Government data, reported by the press
invisible.limit: A part-season count; it shows the gap, not the true toll.
invisible.finding: Between 1 March and 26 July 2026, India’s heat surveillance, covering more than 51,000 reporting units, logged 4,853 heatstroke cases but only 20 heatstroke deaths.

invisible.title: Heat stress reduces productivity among workers in Singapore
invisible.finding: Monitors at 24 indoor and outdoor workplaces in Singapore found workers could face more heat stress than nearby national weather stations reported.

reactive.by: Park and Rubinyi, World Bank working paper, 2026
reactive.title: Urban heat, mortality, and economic costs: evidence from Bangkok, Thailand
reactive.limit: An estimate from a statistical model; the value depends on how a life is priced.
reactive.finding: About 593 deaths a year in Bangkok in 2016–18 were attributable to heat. Valued at 0.1–0.7% of the city’s economy, the upper estimate exceeds the city’s 2020 public health budget.

reactive.title: Adapt Now: A Global Call for Leadership on Climate Resilience
reactive.limit: A broad benefit estimate covering many hazards, not heat alone.
reactive.finding: US$800 million spent on early warning systems in developing countries could avoid US$3–16 billion in losses every year.

reactive.title: Spreading like Wildfire
reactive.limit: About wildfire budgets; we use it as a pattern for heat.
reactive.finding: Direct response typically gets over half of wildfire spending, while planning and prevention get less than 1%.

reactive.title: How is India adapting to heatwaves? An assessment of heat action plans
reactive.limit: Plans as of 2023; several have been updated since.
reactive.finding: Of 37 heat action plans reviewed, 11 discussed funding, and 8 of those simply asked departments to find their own money. Only two included a vulnerability assessment.

reactive.by: Ministry of Home Affairs, reply in India’s Lok Sabha, reported by Down To Earth, 2026
reactive.title: India updates disaster list to include heatwaves and lightning after Finance Commission push
reactive.type: Government statement, reported by the press
reactive.limit: A rule change; how money flows in practice is still to be seen.
reactive.finding: In August 2026 India added heatwaves to its notified natural calamities, so national and state disaster response funds can pay for heatwave relief. Before, states could spend only up to 10% of their response fund on locally declared disasters such as heat. Heat mitigation projects are funded separately, from disaster mitigation funds.

protection.by: Swiss Re Institute sigma, reported by Global Reinsurance
protection.title: Protection gap laid bare as Asian cat losses hit $65bn
protection.type: Industry research, reported by the press
protection.limit: Covers all natural catastrophes, not heat alone; heat losses are rarely insured at all.
protection.finding: Only about 8% of Asia’s US$65 billion in natural catastrophe losses in 2025 was insured. The rest fell on households, businesses and governments.

protection.title: Climate Change & Insurance: Physical risks on the insurance industry
protection.limit: A qualitative assessment; it does not measure the whole cycle in any one place.
protection.reading: We read it as the cycle on the map: repeated heat losses squeeze incomes, cover becomes harder to afford, and more of the loss falls on households and public budgets.
protection.finding: In developing markets with low insurance cover, the protection gap is driven by unaffordable premiums, limited awareness and weak distribution, and heat’s drag on growth and household incomes could shrink the customer base further.
